Triggers.value: The same time of day the event occurred

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

vignette: The afternoon had been ordinary until the streetlights flickered on at precisely 6:15 p.m., casting long shadows across the cracked pavement behind Mele's market. An American of Oceanian heritage, she had been restocking crates of imported produce when two officers approached, their body cameras already recording, their voices sharp and final. When the situation escalated, Mele had felt the sudden, heavy lurch in her stomach, a wave of dizziness that swallowed the world. She could still recall the glare of the overhead bulb, the weight of the officer's hand on her shoulder, the sound of her own breath growing thin, but the moment the patrol car's siren wailed, the memory simply stopped. No matter how hard she tried to grasp what happened next, there was only a blank space. The fragments that remained felt so extreme, so disconnected from the quiet woman who had opened her shop twenty years prior, that she often caught herself wondering if she had imagined the confrontation entirely. She could not find the words to describe the violence, the fear, or the impact; the experience lived entirely in her nerves, in the sudden stillness of her body, in the way her throat tightened when the light began to fail. Over the following months, 6:15 p.m. became a threshold Mele learned to brace against. When the clock on her register ticked toward that hour, the floor would tilt beneath her sneakers, and she would find herself pressing a hand to the glass counter to steady herself. She had come to believe that the darkness behind her store was no longer just an absence of light but a living presence, so she began leaving every porch lamp blazing by late afternoon, shutting her heavy steel shutters before dusk, and locking her office door the moment the sun dipped below the next building. She refused to mark the calendar for the anniversary of the incident, turning her phone to silent and taking long walks through unfamiliar neighborhoods to slip past the date unnoticed. In the quiet hours of the evening, when the shop was empty and the dizziness returned with the cooling air, Mele found herself scanning her inventory sheets with a frantic eye, ordering cases of canned goods, fresh flowers, and specialty items she did not need, swiping her card without pausing to consider the cost or the clutter piling up in the back room. Over time, these patterns settled into the rhythm of her days. Regulars noticed the early closures, the scattered piles of unopened merchandise in the aisles, the way Mele would avoid standing near the rear windows when the street grew dim. She stopped answering the phone after four, let the utility bills settle in the center of her desk, and relied on the repetitive motion of stocking shelves to quiet the rising panic. Her reflection in the darkened register screen no longer looked like the woman who had negotiated leases and managed payroll with steady hands. She had come to believe she was fundamentally inadequate, that her trembling hands and sudden lapses in concentration proved she was a poor coper, someone who could not navigate the ordinary demands of running a business. The constant vigilance-the sense that unseen eyes were tracking her movements through the narrow aisles, the way her pulse would jump at the click of a lock-fueled a quiet terror that her mind was fracturing, that the dizziness and the blank spaces were proof she was going crazy. Now, at sixty-six, the market sits mostly quiet, its shelves misaligned, its accounts overdue, its founder watching the street through a cracked blind. The triggers have not lessened; 6:15 p.m. still arrives with a physical pull, the shadows still feel watchful, and the memory gaps remain stubbornly intact. What brought Mele through the clinic door this morning was a simple, exhausting realization: she could no longer bear the weight of the unspooled days. She is terrified that her fear of losing control will eventually cost her the last thing she has left of her independence, yet she is also desperate for a way to step out of the shadowed hours, to trust her own mind again, and to simply close her register at a reasonable time without bracing for impact.
